title: Witness and Autopsy
premise: When insurance investigator Vesper Vasquez receives two letters in the same mail — one confessing to a hit-and-run that killed a girl named Ada Lark three years ago, the other promising 'the rest of the truth' if Vesper keeps looking — they reopen a case the town of Hollow Creek buried twice. Using their photographic memory, Vesper reconstructs contradictions everyone else chose to forget, discovering Ada's death was staged to hide an inheritance scheme involving the town's founding families, and that the 'dead' witness is alive and hiding in plain sight. The trail leads to Vesper's own late mother, whose filed secrets were never alphabetized by accident. In the end, Vesper must choose between exposing the town's complicity — including their own godfather's — or letting the witness stay dead so she can finally live.
about_author: M. M. Voss is the pen name of a former claims adjuster from rural Ohio who spent eleven years reading other people's worst days in triplicate. They write mysteries about paper trails, small towns, and the things families file away.

chapters.title: Two Envelopes, One Postmark
chapters.summary: Vesper Vasquez's POV. On an ordinary Tuesday, Vesper sorts the morning mail at the Hollow Creek insurance office and finds two letters addressed to them: a signed confession to Ada Lark's hit-and-run, unsigned but dated the night she died, and a second note promising more if Vesper 'keeps looking.' The emotional beat is the crack in a controlled life — memory as both gift and burden.

chapters.title: The Alphabetized Town
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. Establishing chapter: we see how Vesper files the town — every debt, affair, and quiet cruelty memorized verbatim. Their godfather, Sheriff Dale Pruitt, warns them off the letters before they've mentioned them aloud. Beat: unease; someone knows what arrived before Vesper decided to care.

chapters.title: What the Confession Gets Wrong
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. Comparing the confession against the original claim file from memory, Vesper spots errors only the real driver wouldn't make — wrong weather, wrong turn signal. The confession is false, which means it was written to be found. Beat: the investigator's thrill curdling into dread.

chapters.title: Ada's Mother Still Sets Two Plates
chapters.summary: Vesper interviews Ruth Lark, who has never accepted the closed case. Ruth mentions a visitor three years ago — a woman with her mother's voice — whom Vesper cannot place, an unbearable gap in their perfect memory. Beat: grief meeting guilt; the first hole in Vesper's archive.

chapters.title: The Second Letter Arrives Early
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. A second note appears inside Vesper's own locked desk drawer: 'You're faster than he expected.' The antagonist knows their habits intimately. That night someone ransacks the office but takes only Ada's original claim file. Beat: hunted rather than hunting.

chapters.title: Pruitt's Quiet Ledger
chapters.summary: Alternating POV: Sheriff Dale Pruitt, three years earlier. He took the report, saw the tire marks pointing toward the Hollis estate, and chose the version of events that kept Hollow Creek solvent. Beat: complicity rendered sympathetic — a man protecting a town that asked him to.

chapters.title: The Hollis Inheritance
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. Digging into probate records, Vesper learns Ada Lark was the illegitimate granddaughter of dying matriarch Edith Hollis — and that Edith's will, rewritten weeks before Ada's death, named her heir. Beat: motive surfaces; inheritance as murder weapon.

chapters.title: Everyone Swears She's Dead
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. Tracking the 'witness' — a diner waitress named Cora Finch listed as deceased in three documents Vesper can recite from memory — Vesper finds fresh groceries delivered to a house with no living occupant. Beat: hope sharpening into obsession.

chapters.title: A Voice Like My Mother's
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. The woman Ruth described resurfaces in a three-year-old security photo Vester finally places: it's Marion, Vesper's mother, dead by official record for six years. Beat: the personal detonates the professional; the case was always about Vesper.

chapters.title: Interrogating the Godfather
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Vesper confronts Pruitt with the probate timeline; Pruitt admits he was told to close the case by Edith Hollis's lawyer, Ambrose Kell. Pruitt gives Vesper twenty-four hours before he has to arrest them for obstruction. Beat: loyalty fracturing under the weight of duty.

chapters.title: Kell's Beautiful Paperwork
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. At Kell's office, everything is immaculate — too immaculate. Vesper memorizes his filing system and realizes a codicil to Edith's will is missing, replaced by a forgery Vesper's own mother notarized. Beat: cold fury; the law itself was weaponized.

chapters.title: The House With No Occupant
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV, night. Breaking into the Finch house, Vesper finds it lived-in and booby-trapped with tripwires of fishing line — and a wall of clippings about Vesper themselves. Someone has been watching the investigator for years. Beat: reversal; Vesper was always the subject.

chapters.title: Cora, Alive and Counting Days
chapters.summary: Cora Finch's POV. The 'dead' witness reveals herself: she saw the car, saw who drove it, and has survived three years by being legally deceased. She doesn't trust Vesper — until Vesper recites her sister's obituary word-perfect, proving they remember what the town erased. Beat: fragile alliance born of shared memory.

chapters.title: What Cora Saw
chapters.summary: Cora's POV. Her testimony: the driver was young Marcus Hollis, Edith's grandson — but the plan belonged to someone older who stood under the streetlight and watched. She fled when the witness list started shrinking. Beat: the horror isn't the killing; it's the audience.

chapters.title: Marion's Filing System
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. Following their mother's notary stamp through county records, Vesper decodes her habit of misfiling key documents alphabetically wrong — a hidden index only someone with Vesper's memory could read. Beat: inheritance redefined; the true legacy is a map out of the lie.

chapters.title: The Missing Codicil
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. The decoded trail leads to a safe-deposit box holding Edith's real final will — restoring Ada's line, voiding Marcus's inheritance, and naming Marion Vasquez as trustee. Marion didn't die; she disappeared into protective custody after refusing to forge it. Beat: the mother's absence becomes an act of love.

chapters.title: Twenty-Four Hours Expire
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Pruitt arrests Vesper at dawn, hating himself; in the cell, Vesper lays out the entire reconstruction on the floor in evidence-tag order. Pruitt reads it in silence, then unlocks the door: 'I was the second letter writer. I needed you to look.' Beat: betrayal transmuted into partnership.

chapters.title: Ambrose Kell Runs
chapters.summary: Vesper and Pruitt's POV. Kell, tipped off, burns his office and flees toward the state line with Marcus. But Vesper predicted the route from Kell's own travel filings and calls it ahead to the county patrol. Beat: the chase as paperwork made flesh; memory outpacing flight.

chapters.title: The Bridge at Miller's Bend
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV, climax. Kell's car is stopped on the old bridge; Marcus breaks and confesses fully while Kell, cornered, nearly forces Vesper off the rail — until Cora steps out of the fog, alive, and Kell's nerve shatters at the sight of the witness he buried. Beat: the dead returning to testify.

chapters.title: Testimony
chapters.summary: Cora's POV. In the courthouse, Cora testifies under her real name for the first time in three years; Marcus pleads guilty, Kell is indicted, and Edith's true will restores the Lark inheritance. Ruth Lark hears her daughter's name spoken as heir, not victim. Beat: public reckoning; grief given legal form.

chapters.title: Two Plates, Finally One Guest
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. Marion returns, aged and unafraid, and explains why she let Vesper believe she was dead — protection that became cowardice that became shame. They sit across from each other at Ruth's table, four plates now. Beat: belonging rebuilt without erasing the cost.

chapters.title: Witness and Autopsy
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV, coda. Vesper closes the Lark file and opens a new drawer labeled 'Hollow Creek, Unfiled' — choosing to stop alphabetizing the town's sins and start witnessing them. The last letter arrives: blank except for 'Thank you for looking.' Beat: resolution as transformation; memory turned from archive into conscience.
